BREAKING: Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance says it welcomes competition from Elon Musk’s Starlink in India.

Here are the facts:

• Starlink already has 11,000+ satellites in low Earth orbit.

• Starlink has already confirmed that it has developed India-specific security controls and arrangements to keep Indian users’ data within India. It has also built 20 gateway sites across the country.

• Jio has not yet launched any satellites for its own proposed LEO constellation. Its first test launch is reportedly targeted for September 2027, with mass deployment expected to begin in early 2028.

Starlink’s global network is already built. Giving Indians access to Starlink would provide another option for communities where reliable internet access remains a challenge.

More competition can push providers to improve coverage, service, and pricing. Indian consumers deserve that choice.

India should welcome every provider that complies with their rules.

Let them compete in India, and let consumers decide who earns their business.

posts.author: elonmusk
posts.text:
He crashed a million-dollar car he never insured, then told the friend sitting next to him he thought it would never happen to him.

“Watch this.”

That’s what Elon Musk said right before he lost control of his own McLaren F1.

His name is Elon Musk. The year was 2000. He’d just pocketed $22 million selling his first company, Zip2, and used $1 million of it on one of only 106 McLaren F1s ever built. He was driving Peter Thiel to pitch Sequoia Capital for what would become PayPal when Thiel asked what the car could do.

Musk floored it. The F1 had 640 horsepower, weighed barely a ton, and had zero traction control. The back end snapped out instantly, spun the car backward into an embankment, and launched it into the air spinning like a discus.

Both men walked away unhurt. The car didn’t. According to Thiel, Musk’s first words afterward were that he’d read plenty of stories about guys who made money, bought a supercar, and crashed it, and figured it would never happen to him, which is also why he never bought insurance.

They hitchhiked separately to the meeting instead of showing up together.

Honestly, the detail that stays with me isn’t the crash, it’s that he still made the pitch meeting that same day, uninsured wreck and all, like the car was just a line item he’d deal with later.

Would you have skipped insurance on a million-dollar car too, or is that exactly the kind of bet that only looks smart once you’re already a billionaire?

quote.text:
Elon showing Jay Leno the first production unit Tesla Roadster in 2008.

Leno amazed by battery pack with 6,831 lithium-ion cells and gives this take on his first test drive: 

“The good thing with electricity is that you get full torque from 0 RPM. In a gas car, you have to bring the revs to 3 or 4 grand and pop the clutch. Most electric cars feel bottom heavy, but not this. It’s eerily quiet. It’s amazing. All you hear is the wind noise. I like that it’s a sports car, not some dorky little 4-door econo-box.”

***

Just remember.

You aren’t actually driving the Roadster at all.

You are driving a computer and it is telling another computer how to drive the car.

It is steer by wire. Brake by wire. Accelerate by wire.

But you will think it is better to drive than any other.

Isn’t that a mind f###?

Oh and it is SI, formerly known as AI.

I am very emotional tonight. Am thinking about why.

Will write that on the way to the @TheHumanoidHub conference in the morning.

Missed today, had too much to do.

But it goes back to the Tesla owners at the @theXtakeover last week. Several Cybertruck owners told me about getting flipped off in several places in America.

This makes all the shit that I took for years worth it.

I am writing this to you from my 2018 Tesla.

Elon thank you for making our dreams far more interesting tonight.
